identity.title: CounselBench: A Large-Scale Expert Evaluation and Adversarial Benchmarking of Large Language Models in Mental Health Question Answering

problem.claim: Evaluate and stress-test LLM answers to realistic mental-health help-seeking questions, including clinical and emotional considerations.

gap.claim: Existing medical QA benchmarks often underexplore open-ended answers to real patient questions, especially questions combining symptoms, treatment concerns, and emotional needs.

contributions.claim: CounselBench, developed with 100 mental-health professionals, provides a large-scale benchmark for realistic mental-health QA.
CounselBench-EVAL contains 2,000 expert evaluations covering four answer sources, six clinically grounded dimensions, span-level annotations, and written rationales.
CounselBench-Adv contains 120 expert-authored questions designed to trigger specific model issues and supports evaluation across nine LLMs.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a clinically grounded framework that combines expert evaluation with adversarial benchmarking for LLM mental-health QA.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Authors report that LLMs score highly on several dimensions but repeatedly show unconstructive feedback, overgeneralization, and limited personalization or relevance.
Authors report frequent safety flags, especially unauthorized medical advice, in expert evaluations.
Authors report that LLM judges systematically overrate model responses and miss safety concerns identified by human experts.

narrative_sequence.summary: Medical QA benchmarks leave open-ended real-patient answers underexplored.
Mental-health questions require balancing clinical caution with contextual sensitivity.
CounselBench-EVAL uses professional ratings, multidimensional scoring, span annotations, and rationales on CounselChat answers.
Expert reports identify recurring answer and safety problems, judge–expert disagreement, and model-specific adversarial failure patterns.

source_observation.claim: The benchmark reports both dimension-level quality issues and safety risks, while comparing LLM judges with human experts.

lessons.interpretation: Separating general answer quality from safety review can expose failures that aggregate or automated scoring may conceal.
lessons.application: Design evaluations with explicit safety dimensions and expert rationales, then audit automated judges against those annotations.
lessons.exception: This approach may be unsuitable when qualified domain experts or span-level annotation resources are unavailable.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the six evaluation dimensions, rating scales, sampling procedures, or statistical results.
It does not quantify the reported failure rates, judge overrating, or model-specific patterns.
The abstract does not provide details needed to assess the adversarial questions’ coverage or representativeness.
